L1-builder.title: Python modules and project structure
L1-builder.why: Customer integrations grow beyond a single script. A tidy project is easier to review, test, and hand over.
L1-builder.concept: A module is a Python file that groups related code. A package groups modules so the project can be split into clear responsibilities.
L1-builder.analogy: Think of a toolbox with labeled drawers: each drawer holds tools for one kind of task.
L1-builder.example: A customer sync script now has API calls, data cleanup, and logging mixed together. Move each responsibility into a small module and keep one clear entry point.
L1-builder.mistake: Putting every function into one giant file or splitting code into tiny files with no useful boundary.
L1-builder.nextStep: Choose boundaries based on a responsibility, then add a small test around the behavior you moved.
L1-builder.distractor: A module is a remote server that runs Python automatically.

L1-builder.title: REST APIs and requests
L1-builder.why: FDEs often connect a product to systems a customer already uses. HTTP APIs are a common way those systems exchange information.
L1-builder.concept: An API request combines a method, an address, headers, and sometimes a body. The response includes a status and data.
L1-builder.analogy: It is like filling out a service request: the method says what you want done, the address says where, and the body carries details.
L1-builder.example: To create a support ticket, send a POST request to the tickets endpoint with the title and requester in JSON, then inspect the response ID.
L1-builder.mistake: Assuming an endpoint or request shape without checking its documentation and example response.
L1-builder.nextStep: Confirm the method, path, required fields, authentication, and expected response before wiring the call into a workflow.
L1-builder.distractor: A REST API is a graphical page that only people can click.

L1-builder.title: SQL and data tables
L1-builder.why: Customer data often lives in relational databases. SQL helps you inspect and combine that data without changing it accidentally.
L1-builder.concept: A table stores rows of records and columns of fields. SQL statements select, filter, join, or change those records.
L1-builder.analogy: A table is like a labeled spreadsheet; a query is a careful instruction for finding specific rows.
L1-builder.example: A customer asks for paid orders from yesterday. Filter the orders by status and date, then select only the fields needed for the report.
L1-builder.mistake: Running an update or delete before confirming which rows the condition matches.
L1-builder.nextStep: Start with a SELECT using the same WHERE condition, review the returned rows, and use a transaction for approved changes.
L1-builder.distractor: SQL is a file format that stores images and video.

L1-builder.title: Docker and containers
L1-builder.why: A service that works on your laptop can fail on a customer environment when tools or versions differ. Containers make the runtime more repeatable.
L1-builder.concept: A container image packages an application and its required runtime files. A running container is an isolated process created from that image.
L1-builder.analogy: An image is a recipe box with the ingredients and instructions; a container is one prepared serving running on a host.
L1-builder.example: A small API depends on a particular Python version. Build an image with that runtime and start it with the required port and environment settings.
L1-builder.mistake: Putting secrets in the image or assuming a container automatically includes persistent storage.
L1-builder.nextStep: Keep credentials outside the image, document ports and volumes, and test the container with a clean environment.
L1-builder.distractor: Docker is a cloud provider that stores a company’s databases.

L1-builder.title: Cloud basics
L1-builder.why: Customer systems may run on cloud services with different networks, permissions, and costs. FDEs need to ask how those pieces fit together.
L1-builder.concept: Cloud platforms provide computing, storage, networking, and managed services on demand. An account or project groups resources and access policies.
L1-builder.analogy: A cloud account is like a campus: projects are buildings, services are rooms, and permissions decide who can enter.
L1-builder.example: A customer wants an API deployed privately. Identify the cloud account, network boundary, service identity, data store, and people who approve access.
L1-builder.mistake: Choosing a service before understanding region, data rules, networking, and operational ownership.
L1-builder.nextStep: Draw a simple deployment diagram and confirm the customer’s access, location, and cost constraints.
L1-builder.distractor: Cloud means software runs without computers or networks.

L1-builder.title: Ship a small API
L1-builder.why: A small end-to-end service teaches the handoff between code, configuration, and a running environment.
L1-builder.concept: A service should expose a clear interface, validate input, return predictable responses, and provide enough logs to diagnose failures.
L1-builder.analogy: Think of a service like a staffed counter: it needs a clear request form, rules for valid requests, and a receipt showing what happened.
L1-builder.example: Build a health endpoint and a read-only customer status endpoint. Validate the customer ID, return JSON, and log a request ID for each call.
L1-builder.mistake: Returning internal errors to users or deploying before checking the service with realistic inputs.
L1-builder.nextStep: Run local checks, test the error path, document configuration, and verify the deployed endpoint from the expected network.
L1-builder.distractor: An API is complete as soon as its code compiles.

L2-integrator.title: API keys and OAuth
L2-integrator.why: Integrations need a safe way to prove who is calling and what they are allowed to do.
L2-integrator.concept: An API key is a secret credential. OAuth is a flow for granting scoped access without sharing a user’s password with the application.
L2-integrator.analogy: An API key is like a service badge; OAuth is like a visitor pass with a named purpose and limited access.
L2-integrator.example: A customer wants calendar access for one workspace. Ask for the approved OAuth scopes and use the provider’s authorization flow.
L2-integrator.mistake: Committing keys to source control or requesting broad scopes when a narrower permission works.
L2-integrator.nextStep: Store secrets in an approved secret manager, request the least access needed, and plan for rotation and revocation.
L2-integrator.distractor: OAuth is a method for compressing JSON responses.

L2-integrator.title: Webhook foundations
L2-integrator.why: Webhooks let one system notify another when an event happens, avoiding constant polling.
L2-integrator.concept: A webhook is an HTTP request sent to a registered endpoint when a source system emits an event. The receiver should verify and acknowledge it quickly.
L2-integrator.analogy: It is like a doorbell: the sender rings when something happens; the receiver checks who rang and records the visit.
L2-integrator.example: When a payment settles, the billing system sends an event to your endpoint. Verify its signature, store the event ID, and enqueue the work.
L2-integrator.mistake: Trusting a webhook body without checking its signature or doing long processing before responding.
L2-integrator.nextStep: Verify authenticity, acknowledge quickly, and process the event safely in the background.
L2-integrator.distractor: A webhook is a scheduled report that runs once a month.

L2-integrator.title: Pagination
L2-integrator.why: APIs limit how many records they return at once. Pagination helps you retrieve a large dataset in manageable pieces.
L2-integrator.concept: A paginated response contains a page of items and a cursor or next-page link. Continue until the API says there are no more results.
L2-integrator.analogy: It is like reading a book one page at a time and using a bookmark to continue where you left off.
L2-integrator.example: A customer has 4,000 contacts. Request a page, save its cursor, process the contacts, then fetch the next page until the cursor is absent.
L2-integrator.mistake: Assuming the first response contains every record or building a cursor from a guessed page number.
L2-integrator.nextStep: Follow the API’s returned cursor, handle empty pages, and checkpoint progress if a long sync may restart.
L2-integrator.distractor: Pagination is a security rule that blocks users from editing records.

L2-integrator.title: Retries and backoff
L2-integrator.why: Networks and services sometimes fail temporarily. A careful retry can recover; an aggressive retry can make an outage worse.
L2-integrator.concept: Retry transient failures with a limit and increasing delay. Respect retry-after guidance and avoid retrying errors that need a human or input change.
L2-integrator.analogy: If a busy office asks you to come back later, wait a bit longer each time instead of knocking every second.
L2-integrator.example: An API returns 503 and a retry-after value. Pause for the requested period, retry a limited number of times, and record the final outcome.
L2-integrator.mistake: Retrying every error immediately forever, which can create a retry storm.
L2-integrator.nextStep: Set a retry limit, use exponential backoff with jitter, and make the operation safe to repeat.
L2-integrator.distractor: Backoff means increasing the number of parallel requests after a failure.

L2-integrator.title: Idempotency and duplicate safety
L2-integrator.why: Retries, webhook redelivery, and timeouts can cause the same action to arrive more than once.
L2-integrator.concept: An idempotent operation produces the same effect when repeated with the same identity. An idempotency key lets a service recognize a replay.
L2-integrator.analogy: It is like a numbered claim ticket: handing in the same ticket twice should not create two separate claims.
L2-integrator.example: A payment request times out after the provider processed it. Retry using the same idempotency key and check the original result.
L2-integrator.mistake: Generating a new key for every retry or treating a timeout as proof that nothing happened.
L2-integrator.nextStep: Choose a stable key for one intended action, store its outcome, and define how long the key remains valid.
L2-integrator.distractor: Idempotency means every request must return a different result.

L2-integrator.title: ETL pipelines and logs
L2-integrator.why: Data sync work is easier to trust when each step is visible and failures can be traced.
L2-integrator.concept: ETL means extract, transform, and load. Logs record useful events and context so a person can understand what a run did.
L2-integrator.analogy: ETL is like sorting parcels: collect them, label them in the receiving format, then place them on the right shelf.
L2-integrator.example: Read yesterday’s support tickets, map priority values, load them into a reporting table, and log the run ID and number of accepted or rejected rows.
L2-integrator.mistake: Logging tokens or personal data, or swallowing errors so a partial load looks successful.
L2-integrator.nextStep: Log run IDs, counts, durations, and safe error codes; keep sensitive values out of logs.
L2-integrator.distractor: ETL is a type of user interface theme.

L3-ai-engineer.title: Calling an LLM API
L3-ai-engineer.why: Many customer-facing AI features call a language model through an API. The request and response need careful handling like any other integration.
L3-ai-engineer.concept: An LLM API accepts instructions and input, then returns generated output. Track model, token usage, latency, errors, and data handling rules.
L3-ai-engineer.analogy: It is like asking a specialist a question: the answer depends on the instructions, context, and time available.
L3-ai-engineer.example: Send a short support summary request with only approved case details, set a timeout, and record safe usage metrics.
L3-ai-engineer.mistake: Assuming the output is always correct or sending customer data before confirming policy and retention.
L3-ai-engineer.nextStep: Start with minimal approved data, handle failures, and measure quality, cost, and latency for real examples.
L3-ai-engineer.distractor: An LLM API guarantees a factually correct answer for every prompt.

L3-ai-engineer.title: Prompting for useful results
L3-ai-engineer.why: Clear instructions help a model respond in a format and style that fits a customer workflow.
L3-ai-engineer.concept: A prompt gives the model a task, relevant context, constraints, and a desired output. Examples can clarify the expected pattern.
L3-ai-engineer.analogy: A prompt is like a good work brief: it says what done means and what boundaries to respect.
L3-ai-engineer.example: Ask for a concise summary using only the supplied notes, identify unknown details explicitly, and use headings for decision, evidence, and open questions.
L3-ai-engineer.mistake: Adding vague goals or private data while expecting the model to infer unstated rules.
L3-ai-engineer.nextStep: Specify the task, context, boundaries, output format, and how to handle uncertainty; test against varied examples.
L3-ai-engineer.distractor: Prompting is choosing a longer instruction regardless of the task.

L3-ai-engineer.title: Structured model output
L3-ai-engineer.why: Software needs predictable fields to use model responses safely in a workflow.
L3-ai-engineer.concept: Structured output constrains a model response to a defined shape, often JSON with required fields and allowed values.
L3-ai-engineer.analogy: It is like a form with labeled boxes: each answer has a place, and missing information can be marked clearly.
L3-ai-engineer.example: Extract a date, issue type, and confidence from a ticket. Validate the response against a schema before creating a downstream record.
L3-ai-engineer.mistake: Assuming valid-looking JSON is semantically correct or using an unchecked field to trigger an important action.
L3-ai-engineer.nextStep: Validate types and allowed values, handle missing or invalid fields, and require confirmation for consequential actions.
L3-ai-engineer.distractor: Structured output removes the need to test model behavior.

L3-ai-engineer.title: Embeddings and similarity
L3-ai-engineer.why: Search over customer documents often needs to find meaning, not just exact word matches.
L3-ai-engineer.concept: An embedding maps text into a list of numbers that represents aspects of its meaning. Similar vectors can indicate related content.
L3-ai-engineer.analogy: Imagine each paragraph placed on a map: related ideas land near one another, even when their exact words differ.
L3-ai-engineer.example: A user asks “How do I reset access?” A semantic search can find a document titled “Account recovery” even though the wording differs.
L3-ai-engineer.mistake: Treating similarity as proof that a document is correct, current, or allowed for this user.
L3-ai-engineer.nextStep: Filter by permissions and metadata, inspect retrieved passages, and measure search quality using real questions.
L3-ai-engineer.distractor: An embedding is an encrypted copy of a paragraph.

L3-ai-engineer.title: Retrieval-augmented generation
L3-ai-engineer.why: A model may not know a customer’s private or recent information. Retrieval can provide approved source material for an answer.
L3-ai-engineer.concept: RAG retrieves relevant documents and supplies their passages as context for a model to answer from.
L3-ai-engineer.analogy: It is like an open-book exam: the answer should be grounded in the pages provided, and the reader should show which pages were used.
L3-ai-engineer.example: Search a permitted policy collection, pass the best matching passages to the model, and display links to those passages with the answer.
L3-ai-engineer.mistake: Assuming retrieval guarantees a correct answer or failing to enforce document access before search.
L3-ai-engineer.nextStep: Check access before retrieval, evaluate source relevance, cite evidence, and let the system say when evidence is missing.
L3-ai-engineer.distractor: RAG means retraining a model on every customer question.

L3-ai-engineer.title: Tool calling and evaluations
L3-ai-engineer.why: A model can decide that a tool would help, but tool calls still need validation and clear limits.
L3-ai-engineer.concept: Tool calling lets a model request a defined function. An evaluation checks model behavior against examples and expected criteria.
L3-ai-engineer.analogy: The model is a dispatcher; tools are workers with specific job descriptions, and evaluations are practice inspections.
L3-ai-engineer.example: The assistant proposes a read-only order lookup. Validate the order ID and user access, run the lookup, then show the result with its source.
L3-ai-engineer.mistake: Letting model-generated arguments directly perform a sensitive action without checking permissions or results.
L3-ai-engineer.nextStep: Keep tools narrow, validate every argument, log actions, and run a representative evaluation set before release.
L3-ai-engineer.distractor: An evaluation is a single successful demo with no expected answers.

L4-field-operator.title: Security fundamentals
L4-field-operator.why: FDEs work with customer data and systems. Safe defaults protect the customer and the team delivering the solution.
L4-field-operator.concept: Security reduces risk through identity checks, least privilege, encryption, safe defaults, and a clear record of important actions.
L4-field-operator.analogy: It is like a building with a visitor desk, locked rooms, and a sign-in record rather than one key for everyone.
L4-field-operator.example: A support tool needs to read ticket summaries. Grant its service identity read-only access to that workspace and log access decisions.
L4-field-operator.mistake: Giving broad access because it is faster during a demo and forgetting to remove it later.
L4-field-operator.nextStep: Map what data is used, who needs access, and how access is granted, reviewed, and revoked.
L4-field-operator.distractor: Security means hiding the application URL.

L4-field-operator.title: Tenant isolation and secrets
L4-field-operator.why: A multi-customer product must keep each customer’s data and credentials separated.
L4-field-operator.concept: Tenant isolation checks that every request is scoped to the correct customer. Secrets are credentials stored and delivered through a protected mechanism.
L4-field-operator.analogy: Each customer gets a separate locked room; a secret is a key stored in a controlled key cabinet.
L4-field-operator.example: A user requests an export. Derive the tenant from the authenticated session, verify access, and fetch only that tenant’s records.
L4-field-operator.mistake: Trusting a tenant ID supplied by the browser or storing a token in source code.
L4-field-operator.nextStep: Enforce tenant scope on the server side, test cross-tenant access attempts, and rotate exposed credentials.
L4-field-operator.distractor: Tenant isolation is achieved by putting a customer name in the page title.

L4-field-operator.title: CI/CD and safe releases
L4-field-operator.why: Customer-facing changes should be checked before they reach a live environment.
L4-field-operator.concept: Continuous integration runs checks on code changes. Continuous delivery prepares a tested change for release through a controlled process.
L4-field-operator.analogy: It is like inspecting a package at each checkpoint before it leaves the warehouse.
L4-field-operator.example: A pull request triggers lint, unit tests, build, and a smoke test. A release then promotes the reviewed artifact to the customer environment.
L4-field-operator.mistake: Treating a green build as proof that every customer workflow works or releasing without a rollback plan.
L4-field-operator.nextStep: Make checks repeatable, review the diff, deploy gradually when possible, and know how to reverse a bad release.
L4-field-operator.distractor: CI/CD means pushing every local edit directly to production.

L4-field-operator.title: Kubernetes basics
L4-field-operator.why: Some customers use Kubernetes to run and manage containerized services across a cluster.
L4-field-operator.concept: A cluster runs workloads described as desired state. Kubernetes controllers work to keep the actual state close to that description.
L4-field-operator.analogy: It is like a venue manager keeping the requested number of staffed rooms available as people arrive and leave.
L4-field-operator.example: A deployment asks for two copies of an API. A service gives those copies a stable network address while Kubernetes replaces an unhealthy copy.
L4-field-operator.mistake: Changing a live pod by hand and assuming the change will survive a replacement.
L4-field-operator.nextStep: Understand the deployment, service, configuration, and health checks before investigating a workload.
L4-field-operator.distractor: Kubernetes is a programming language for container images.

L4-field-operator.title: On-premises and air-gapped deployments
L4-field-operator.why: Some customers run software in their own data center or a network that cannot connect to the public internet.
L4-field-operator.concept: An on-premises deployment runs on customer-managed infrastructure. An air-gapped environment has no direct connection to an external network.
L4-field-operator.analogy: It is like delivering a sealed kit to a secure site where outside delivery services cannot enter.
L4-field-operator.example: The customer needs a release package in an isolated network. Confirm approved transfer, signatures, dependencies, update procedure, and support path.
L4-field-operator.mistake: Assuming the environment can download images, call external services, or receive updates automatically.
L4-field-operator.nextStep: Inventory dependencies and approvals early, then test the exact installation path the customer permits.
L4-field-operator.distractor: Air-gapped means the server is connected to a faster Wi-Fi network.

L4-field-operator.title: Observability and incidents
L4-field-operator.why: When a customer reports a problem, you need evidence about what the system did and how users were affected.
L4-field-operator.concept: Logs record events, metrics summarize measurements over time, and traces connect work across services. Incident response coordinates impact reduction and recovery.
L4-field-operator.analogy: Logs are individual notes, metrics are a dashboard of vital signs, and traces follow one request through the system.
L4-field-operator.example: A customer sees slow syncs. Compare request duration metrics, inspect a trace for the slow dependency, and update the incident timeline.
L4-field-operator.mistake: Changing several systems at once before preserving evidence or communicating customer impact.
L4-field-operator.nextStep: Confirm impact, assign an owner, use observable evidence, communicate updates, and record follow-up actions.
L4-field-operator.distractor: Observability means collecting every customer field in a log.

L5-fde-hero.title: Customer discovery
L5-fde-hero.why: An FDE needs to understand the real workflow before deciding what to build.
L5-fde-hero.concept: Discovery uncovers users, goals, current steps, pain points, data, constraints, and how success will be measured.
L5-fde-hero.analogy: It is like mapping a route with the person who takes it every day before you design a shortcut.
L5-fde-hero.example: A team asks for automated invoice review. Ask who reviews invoices, what exceptions matter, which systems are involved, and what result would save time safely.
L5-fde-hero.mistake: Taking the requested feature as the problem statement without watching the current workflow.
L5-fde-hero.nextStep: Ask open questions, request a recent example, and summarize what you heard for the customer to correct.
L5-fde-hero.distractor: Discovery is a presentation where the engineer lists product features.

L5-fde-hero.title: Scoping and priorities
L5-fde-hero.why: Customer requests often exceed the time or information available. A clear scope gives both sides a realistic first outcome.
L5-fde-hero.concept: Scope defines what will be delivered, what is excluded, assumptions, risks, owners, and a way to decide whether the result worked.
L5-fde-hero.analogy: It is like agreeing on a first trail section before promising to build the whole mountain road.
L5-fde-hero.example: A customer asks for five dashboards by Friday. Agree on one decision the dashboard must support, the data needed, and a demoable first version.
L5-fde-hero.mistake: Promising every requested item or silently changing the deadline and quality bar.
L5-fde-hero.nextStep: Write a small outcome, its acceptance check, dependencies, and explicit non-goals; review them with stakeholders.
L5-fde-hero.distractor: Scope is a list of every idea anyone has mentioned.

L5-fde-hero.title: Stakeholder communication
L5-fde-hero.why: A deployment can affect users, technical owners, security teams, and decision makers. Clear updates keep people aligned.
L5-fde-hero.concept: Useful stakeholder communication adjusts detail to the audience while keeping impact, decision, owner, and next update clear.
L5-fde-hero.analogy: It is like a control tower: each person needs the right signal at the right time, not every radio conversation.
L5-fde-hero.example: A launch is delayed by a data permission. Tell the sponsor the user impact and revised plan; give the technical owner the exact permission and test needed.
L5-fde-hero.mistake: Sending a long technical log to everyone or hiding a delay until the final meeting.
L5-fde-hero.nextStep: State what changed, why it matters, who owns the next action, and when people will hear from you again.
L5-fde-hero.distractor: Communication is complete when a message has been sent, regardless of whether it was understood.

L5-fde-hero.title: Demos and handover
L5-fde-hero.why: A demo should help a customer judge a result, and a handover should help them operate it afterwards.
L5-fde-hero.concept: A good demo follows a realistic task and shows evidence of value. A handover covers operation, limits, owners, and support steps.
L5-fde-hero.analogy: A demo is a guided test drive; a handover is giving the driver the map, keys, and maintenance notes.
L5-fde-hero.example: Show a user submitting one real example, reviewing the result, and correcting an exception. Then show where to find logs and who owns failed cases.
L5-fde-hero.mistake: Showing only a polished happy path or ending without documenting known gaps.
L5-fde-hero.nextStep: Agree on the demo goal, use representative data, show one failure path, and leave concise operating notes.
L5-fde-hero.distractor: A demo is a collection of slides describing features the customer cannot try.

L5-fde-hero.title: Case studies and portfolio
L5-fde-hero.why: A portfolio gives interviewers concrete evidence that you can understand a problem and deliver a working result.
L5-fde-hero.concept: A strong case study explains the user problem, constraints, your choices, the result, and what you would improve. Protect private customer details.
L5-fde-hero.analogy: It is like a field notebook: show the route, decisions, evidence, and lessons rather than only a photo of the finish line.
L5-fde-hero.example: Describe a sample integration with a diagram, a short demo, test coverage, setup instructions, and a clear note about what is simulated.
L5-fde-hero.mistake: Claiming unverified impact or publishing customer data and credentials to make a project look impressive.
L5-fde-hero.nextStep: Use synthetic data, explain your personal contribution, and link to a reproducible project with a readable README.
L5-fde-hero.distractor: A portfolio is a list of technologies with no example of how you used them.

L5-fde-hero.title: Interviews and negotiation
L5-fde-hero.why: FDE interviews test both technical judgment and how you work with people. Preparation helps you explain your reasoning clearly.
L5-fde-hero.concept: Use specific examples to show discovery, implementation, trade-offs, communication, and outcomes. Negotiation is a respectful conversation about the role and offer terms.
L5-fde-hero.analogy: An interview is a working session, not a memory contest; negotiation is aligning expectations before starting a partnership.
L5-fde-hero.example: For an ambiguous customer scenario, ask clarifying questions, state assumptions, sketch a safe first step, and explain how you would validate it.
L5-fde-hero.mistake: Pretending to know an answer, giving only abstract claims, or accepting terms before understanding them.
L5-fde-hero.nextStep: Practice concise stories, ask about responsibilities and support, and compare the written offer with your priorities.
L5-fde-hero.distractor: Negotiation means making an ultimatum before learning the role details.
